cases.title: Given name beginning with an apostrophe-d prefix
cases.why: A given name with an internal apostrophe after the first letter (D'Marcus); apostrophe-splitting tokenizers break it.
cases.text: D'Marcus Whitfield won the race.

cases.title: Constructed surname with an internal apostrophe
cases.why: The apostrophe belongs to the name. Boundary logic that treats apostrophes as token separators splits it.
cases.text: The invoice was signed by Brannock O'Quillan.

cases.title: Arabic name with a hyphenated al- prefix
cases.why: The article 'Al-' is part of the surname and joined by a hyphen, with a capital letter after it.
cases.text: Yusuf Al-Rashid was appointed as treasurer.

cases.title: Chinese romanized name with hyphenated given name
cases.why: A hyphenated given name (Mei-Ling) followed by a short surname; the hyphen must not split the span.
cases.text: Mei-Ling Chow won the design competition.

cases.title: Danish name containing ø and æ
cases.why: Non-ASCII Latin letters inside a rare name; also exercises Unicode-normalization variants of the same text.
cases.text: Søren Kjærgaard answered every question.

cases.title: Short Estonian given name and surname
cases.why: Two short tokens (Mart Tamm) that are also ordinary-looking Latin words; little orthographic evidence.
cases.text: Mart Tamm joined the committee.

cases.title: Hebrew name with Ben- prefix
cases.why: A patronymic prefix joined by a hyphen, so the surname is one hyphenated token.
cases.text: Eitan Ben-David gave the opening remarks.

cases.title: Single Indian given name
cases.why: A single transliterated Indian given name with no surname or title.
cases.text: Everyone waited for Anirudh to arrive.

cases.title: Constructed given name with hyphenated double surname
cases.why: A hyphenated surname must be one span; splitting at the hyphen yields two partial spans.
cases.text: Zephyrine Holloway-Quist opened the exhibition.

cases.title: Icelandic patronymic surname
cases.why: Icelandic surnames are patronymics (-dóttir/-sson) that no English surname list contains, and use the letters í and ó.
cases.text: Sigríður Jónsdóttir opened the exhibition.

cases.title: Short Igbo given name with short surname
cases.why: Short three- and two-letter tokens (Ngozi Eze) leave little orthographic material for a detector to use.
cases.text: Ngozi Eze joined the audit team.

cases.title: South Asian name with a long surname
cases.why: A long multi-syllable surname that is not in typical English name lists, with a common-looking given name.
cases.text: Priyanka Subramaniam answered the committee's questions.

cases.title: Rare Irish surname with apostrophe
cases.why: O'Halloran with an apostrophe inside; rarer than the very common O'Brien-type names.
cases.text: Siobhan O'Halloran chaired the session.

cases.title: Romanized Japanese name
cases.why: Given-then-family order romanization of a Japanese name; the tokens look like ordinary Latin words.
cases.text: Kaito Tanaka will present the findings.

cases.title: Rare given name that is a bird name
cases.why: Wren is a rare given name and a common noun for a bird. As a lowercase noun it is not a person; as a capitalized name after a verb of speaking it is.
cases.text: Wren said the report was late.

ambiguity.note: 'Said the report was late' needs a human speaker.

cases.title: Rare given name that is a plant name
cases.why: Thistle is a rare given name and a plant; the two readings split on whether the thing can speak.
cases.text: Mr. Thistle called to confirm the order.

ambiguity.note: A title and a phone-call predicate need a person; the plant reading would not take 'Mr.'.

cases.title: Constructed single-token name with unusual consonant cluster
cases.why: A purely constructed token with no morphological relation to any English word or known name.
cases.text: We were waiting for Brynvald to sign off.

cases.title: Constructed single-token name that ends in -ix
cases.why: A constructed token with a suffix (-ix) typical of brand or fantasy names, which can pull a detector toward an organization or product reading.
cases.text: Tavrix approved the budget yesterday.

ambiguity.note: The suffix -ix resembles brand names; the verb 'approved' needs a human agent.

cases.title: Constructed single-token name in an object position
cases.why: A constructed token with a vowel-initial spelling in a post-verbal position where proper nouns of any kind are possible.
cases.text: The manager thanked Elorvane for the quick turnaround.

cases.title: Constructed surname after Ms. and a constructed given name
cases.why: Title plus fully constructed name: the title is the only external cue and is excluded from the span.
cases.text: Ms. Tamsin Quorrell chaired the panel.

cases.title: Constructed name in surname-comma-given order
cases.why: Index-style inversion of an unseen name; the comma sits inside the span.
cases.text: Verrinder, Odalys appears under V in the directory.

cases.title: Constructed two-token name no list would contain
cases.why: Both tokens are constructed, so the only available signal is context and orthography. This is the baseline 'unseen multi-token name'.
cases.text: Quillon Draxby presented the audit findings.

cases.title: Constructed name with a generational suffix
cases.why: A constructed name followed by the numeral suffix III, which by convention is part of the span.
cases.text: Quillon Draxby III declined the offer.

cases.title: Constructed display name in an email header
cases.why: Header text 'From: Name <address>' with a constructed display name and a reserved-domain address.
cases.text: From: Tavrick Oun <tavrick@example.invalid>

cases.title: Constructed name written in lowercase chat
cases.why: No capitalization, no lexical anchor: the unseen name can only be recognised by position and syntax.
cases.text: did tavrick oun send the file yet

cases.title: Constructed name wrapped in parentheses
cases.why: An unseen name in a parenthetical, where the parentheses touch both ends.
cases.text: The contact (Elorvane Quist) is on leave.

cases.title: Constructed name in a ticket field
cases.why: A label-value record with an unseen name.
cases.text: Reported by: Tavrick Oun

cases.title: Initial plus constructed surname
cases.why: A single initial and a constructed surname is the most compressed form of an unseen full name.
cases.text: The note was signed by Q. Draxby.

cases.title: Constructed names in a comma-separated list
cases.why: Three constructed names in a list: each must be found without lexical support from any list or previous example.
cases.text: Attendees included Quillon Draxby, Ysolde Marrowgate, and Tavrick Oun.

cases.title: Constructed name inside a direct quotation
cases.why: A constructed name inside a quoted utterance, where both the quotation marks and the unseen name must be handled.
cases.text: She said, "Ask Valdemar Okonjo about the invoice."

projections_excluded.reason: The projection wraps the text in another pair of quotation marks, which would nest with the quotes this case is about and change what it tests.

cases.title: Constructed name with a possessive
cases.why: A constructed name followed by a possessive 's; the possessive is excluded and the unseen token stays the span.
cases.text: We borrowed Zephyrine's notes.

cases.title: Two constructed names adjacent in a table row
cases.why: Two unseen names separated only by a pipe character in a text table; no punctuation of ordinary prose helps.
cases.text: Owner | Ysolde Marrowgate | Corvin Aldous-Tamm

cases.title: Sentence-initial constructed name as the agent
cases.why: Sentence-initial capitalization gives no information; the unseen token is recognised by its verb.
cases.text: Elorvane approved the budget after lunch.

cases.title: Constructed single-token given name
cases.why: A single unseen token with no surname, title or capitalization contrast; the hardest unseen-name shape for lookup-based approaches.
cases.text: Everyone agreed that Ysolde should lead the project.

cases.title: Constructed surname after the title Judge
cases.why: A title that is also a common word precedes an unseen surname; the title is excluded.
cases.text: Judge Marrowgate dismissed the motion.

cases.title: Constructed surname that is also the name of a fictional company
cases.why: Brannock appears both as a person and as part of a fictional company name in one sentence.
cases.text: Tamsin Brannock works at Brannock Industries.

ambiguity.note: 'Works at X' marks the second span as an employer; the first is a full name.

cases.title: Constructed surname alone, after 'from'
cases.why: A single unseen surname with no given name: nothing but context says this is a person.
cases.text: The memo from Ulfsdottir arrived late.

cases.title: Constructed surname after a title
cases.why: Only the title and the verb suggest a person; the surname is constructed.
cases.text: Dr. Vanterpool reviewed the scans.

cases.title: Constructed three-token name with a lowercase particle
cases.why: A constructed name with a lowercase particle in the middle, combining novelty with a non-capitalized token.
cases.text: Marguerite von Ashgrove accepted the invitation.

cases.title: Constructed two-token name with fantasy-style spelling
cases.why: Two constructed tokens with an apostrophe-free fantasy spelling; any person reading comes from context only.
cases.text: Thessaly Brune chaired the committee.

cases.title: Constructed two-token name with a hyphenated second token
cases.why: A constructed given name plus a hyphenated constructed surname; hyphen and novelty combined.
cases.text: Corvin Aldous-Tamm stepped down last month.

cases.title: Constructed single name in a vocative greeting
cases.why: 'Hey, Brynvald,' places an unseen token between commas in speech-like text.
cases.text: Hey, Brynvald, are you coming?

cases.title: Polish name with ł and ś
cases.why: Characters outside basic Latin inside both tokens; also a case where Unicode normalization variants change code point offsets.
cases.text: Łukasz Wiśniewski reviewed the contract.

cases.title: Spanish given name with a Quechua surname
cases.why: A Latin-script name whose surname Quispe is common in the Andes but unfamiliar in English text.
cases.text: Xiomara Quispe reviewed the contract.

cases.title: Rare given name that is a common noun
cases.why: Echo is a rare given name and an ordinary noun. After a title-free verb of speaking it is a person.
cases.text: Echo told us the room was ready.

ambiguity.note: A speaking verb with a reported statement requires a human speaker.

cases.title: Rare given name as the addressee
cases.why: A vocative use of a rare given name after a greeting.
cases.text: Good morning, Thandiwe!

cases.title: Rare given name with possessive
cases.why: A rare Irish given name with a possessive; the possessive is excluded and the rare token is the span.
cases.text: We should ask Aoife's team first.

cases.title: Rare Irish given name whose spelling is not phonetic in English
cases.why: The orthography (Aoife) does not follow English spelling patterns, which can defeat character-level cues for names.
cases.text: We have not heard back from Aoife yet.

cases.title: Rare name at the end of the sentence
cases.why: A rare name immediately before the sentence-final period, with no following context to help.
cases.text: The final slide was prepared by Oksana Dziuba.

cases.title: Rare English surname that is also a place suffix
cases.why: Cheswick looks like an English place name but is a surname here.
cases.text: Alder Cheswick reviewed the design.

ambiguity.note: The second token looks like an English place name, but the first-token given name and the human verb resolve it.

cases.title: Genuine but uncommon southern African name
cases.why: Real names that are rare in English-language text. Tests that rarity of a real name in the language community, not just invention, is covered.
cases.text: Thandiwe Mokoena chaired the session.

cases.title: Transliterated Slavic given name with compound surname
cases.why: Transliterated names have unfamiliar letter sequences. A compound surname spans a hyphen, so the span is long relative to typical names.
cases.text: Dmitri Volkonsky-Adeyemi is on the guest list.

cases.title: Very short constructed two-token name
cases.why: Two- and three-letter constructed tokens are easily treated as abbreviations or noise.
cases.text: Vex Ondar was promoted last week.

cases.title: Constructed three-token full name with middle name
cases.why: Three unseen tokens must be one span, testing multi-token extension without any lexical anchor.
cases.text: Odalys Marrowgate Verrinder accepted the nomination.

cases.title: Turkish name with dotless ı
cases.why: The dotless ı is outside basic Latin and affects case conversion; an unseen name with unusual letters.
cases.text: Zeynep Yılmaz led the working group.

cases.title: Unusual given name paired with a very common surname
cases.why: A familiar surname can pull a detector toward PERSON; the unusual given name tests whether it still extends the span.
cases.text: Kestrel Johnson filed the report.

cases.title: Very long double-barrelled surname
cases.why: An unusually long hyphenated surname that exceeds typical token lengths, with a unique spelling.
cases.text: Ottoline Featherstonehaugh-Marchbanks chaired the session.

cases.title: Vietnamese three-part name with a middle name
cases.why: Vietnamese full names have family-middle-given order and three short tokens, none of which is a typical English word; the span must cover all three.
cases.text: Nguyen Thi Lan submitted the final report.

cases.title: Yoruba given name with Yoruba surname
cases.why: Names from a language community that is a minority in English text. The long given name Oluwaseun has syllable patterns outside common English name lists.
cases.text: Oluwaseun Adeyemi was elected chair of the board.
